newsitem.title: INDIA: India I-Sec sees little rise in bank credit demand.
newsitem.headline: India I-Sec sees little rise in bank credit demand.

text.p: Investment firm ICICI Securities and Finance Company Ltd (I-Sec) said it did not believe that there has been a genuine increase in demand for money in the first quarter of 1997/98 (April-March).
I-Sec was referring to the Reserve Bank of India (RBI)'s recent statement on improvement in bank credit in its its latest Debt Market Update released on Wednesday.

An RBI statement last week said the relative credit situation has shown a significant improvement over the previous year. It said the decline in non-food credit for the first quarter of 1997/98 was 40.64 billion rupees compared with 72.20 billion in the corresponding period in the previous year.

Also, banks' investment in public sector bonds, corporate debentures and commercial papers have increased by 26.82 billion rupees compared to an increase of 8.70 billion rupees in the year-ago period, the RBI had said.

"While the sharp increase in investments in corporate debt is largely due to the withdrawal of the five percent restriction in the slack season credit policy, this effectively forms part of advances to industrial sector and needs to be taken into consideration for computing the credit-deposit ratio," the I-Sec report said.
I-Sec said a true picture will be available only if the components of these advances are known.

"If a large chunk of the incremental advances are flowing to oil companies to fund the huge oil pool deficit, this would be 'non-productive' credit and would in no way boost industrial activity," the report said.
"Another strong chance is that a fairly large portion of the incremental credit is being used to refinance earlier high cost borrowings which again would fail to spur industrial activity."
"Taking all these factors into consideration, it is hard to believe that there has been a genuine increase in demand for money in the first quarter," it added.
With yield on 10-year government security fast approaching 12 percent levels, the spread between banks' prime lending rates (PLRs) and gilt returns is widening, I-Sec said.
"Hence lending to the commercial sector has become relatively more attractive and we are likely to see banks' increase their investments in corporate debt at interest rates close to their PLRs."
